title: Paper bombs ride the jet stream

facts.text: Before dawn on 3 November 1944, the Imperial Japanese Army launched its first Fu-Go balloon bombs toward North America. The date was the birthday of the late Emperor Meiji.
The balloons were launched from three sites on the Pacific coast of Honshu: Otsu in Ibaraki, Ichinomiya in Chiba, and Nakoso in Fukushima. Together they could launch about 200 balloons a day.
The idea was to let the winter jet stream, a fast river of wind about 30,000 feet up, carry the unmanned balloons more than 5,000 miles across the Pacific in a few days.
Each balloon was filled with hydrogen and made of tough paper from the kozo mulberry bush, glued in layers with a paste made from konnyaku, a starchy root.

At night the gas cooled and the balloon sank. A barometer device then fired a small charge to drop a sandbag from a ring hung below, and the balloon climbed again. If it rose too high, a valve let out hydrogen.
When the last sandbags were gone, the same ring dropped the bombs, and a charge was meant to destroy the balloon. A typical load was one antipersonnel bomb of about 15 kg and four incendiaries.
On 4 November 1944, the day after the first launch, the U.S. Navy found a large Japanese balloon floating off the California coast. It was the first sign of the campaign.
Japan launched more than 9,000 balloons between November 1944 and April 1945. Only about 300 were found or seen in North America, from Alaska and Canada to Mexico and as far east as Michigan.
On 4 January 1945 the U.S. Office of Censorship asked newspapers and radio not to report the balloons, so Japan would never learn whether they were working.

On 5 May 1945, on Gearhart Mountain near Bly, Oregon, a church picnic group found a grounded balloon. Its bomb exploded and killed Elsie Mitchell, 26 and pregnant, and five children: Dick Patzke, 14, Joan Patzke, 13, Jay Gifford, 13, Edward Engen, 13, and Sherman Shoemaker, 11.
Her husband, the Reverend Archie Mitchell, was parking the car and survived. The six were the only people killed by enemy action in the continental United States during the war.
Japan stopped launching in April 1945, short of paper and hydrogen and with no news of any results. The U.S. War Department made the danger public on 22 May 1945.

declassified.fact: Decades after the war, women who had helped build the balloons as Japanese schoolgirls folded 1,000 paper cranes for Bly, Oregon, as a symbol of regret for the six lives lost there. The gesture grew out of letters between the women and Bly residents, brought together by Yuzuru "John" Takeshita.

film.shot_notes: U.S. Army film 'Japanese Paper Balloon' (no captions). The file is the stretch from 0:25 to 3:00 of the NARA reel, re-encoded at 30 fps. File times: about 0:05 to 0:25 a balloon drifting in the sky over water and land, the best moving opener; about 0:35 a downed envelope on the ground seen from the air; 0:50 to 1:10 an animated map of the balloon's path from Japan across the Pacific to North America; 1:20 to 1:55 an inflated balloon aloft, filmed from the ground; about 1:35 servicemen examine the ballast ring and its hanging gear; 2:05 to 2:35 a man unfolds the paper envelope. The rest of the reel (not in the file) is a classroom demonstration of the release mechanism. The audio track has faint low level sound, not identified as speech or period sound; treat it as silent unless checked.
film.license: U.S. Army Signal Corps film, U.S. government work, public domain (NARA's blanket 'possibly copyright' flag on 111-ADC reels)

Before dawn on 3 November 1944, the Imperial Japanese Army launched its first Fu-Go balloon bombs toward North America. Each balloon was made of kozo mulberry paper and filled with hydrogen, and the winter jet stream was meant to carry it more than 5,000 miles across the Pacific in a few days. This is real U.S. Army film of a captured balloon, dated 1946 by the National Archives: a balloon in flight, the film's own map of its route, and the ring that carried the ballast and bombs. It does not show the 1944 launch. The original film is silent.

body:
Before dawn, Japan released the first of more than 9,000 paper balloons carrying bombs, and let the wind do the rest.

3 November 1944. From three sites on the Pacific coast of Honshu, the Imperial Japanese Army launched its first Fu-Go balloon bombs toward North America. The plan was for the winter jet stream, about 30,000 feet up, to carry them more than 5,000 miles across the Pacific in a few days.

Each balloon was tough mulberry paper, glued with a paste made from a starchy root and filled with hydrogen. At night the gas cooled and the balloon sank, so a barometer fired a charge to drop a sandbag, and it climbed again. When the last sandbags were gone, the bombs fell.

The next day the U.S. Navy found one floating off California. Only about 300 were ever found or seen in North America, and newspapers were asked to stay silent so Japan would never learn whether they worked.

On 5 May 1945, near Bly, Oregon, a church picnic group found one on the ground. Its bomb killed Elsie Mitchell and five children, the only people killed by enemy action in the continental United States during the war.
